title: Small and regular
hookLine: a small weekly act tends to last longer than a rare grand one

cards: Picture two people. The first, once a year, does something huge: runs a marathon for charity, flies across the world to build a school. Photos, speeches, a glow that lasts a month.
The second visits the same elderly neighbor every Tuesday for twenty minutes. No photos. Nobody claps.
Ten years later, which one has changed more, in the world and in themselves?

teach.b: Two old voices say something surprisingly similar here, each from inside its own tradition.
In Islam, a well-known hadith, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, tells that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was asked which deeds are most beloved to God.

His answer: the ones done most regularly, even if they are small. And Maimonides, whose ladder of giving came up earlier this week, makes a related point in his commentary on a teaching in the Mishnah.
Giving a thousand coins to one person in one go, he says, doesn't shape your character the way giving one coin a thousand times does. The repetition is what trains the heart.
Each tradition has its own reasons, rooted in its own faith, and they aren't saying the same thing in the same way. But they meet on a very practical point. The grand gesture happens to you once.

The small, regular act happens a hundred times, and slowly it changes who you are. It's also more likely to last. A huge commitment is easy to start and hard to keep; when life gets busy, it's the first thing to go.
A small one fits into a real week. That's why this week's practice was one act a week, never one heroic day.
And the simplest trick for keeping it is almost boring: give it a slot.
Same day, same time, in the calendar like a dentist appointment. Then, when the day comes, you don't have to decide. You just go.

how: Many people of every faith and none keep a standing weekly slot for service, like a Tuesday shift at a shelter or a regular visit to a neighbor, so it happens without deciding each time.

practice: Look back at this week, the act you planned, the anonymous gift, the question you asked, and find the one that could repeat.
Picture next week's calendar, pick a day and an hour that's usually free, and see yourself there doing the same small thing again. Let it feel ordinary, like brushing your teeth; that's the goal.
